extracted.intended_audience: school students, coaches, and organizers interested in the Tournament of Towns (math competition)
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of the Tournament of Towns competition format, scoring, participant divisions, problem style, and awards for an international school-level mathematics contest originating in Russia. Useful for prospective contestants, coaches, and local committees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round structure
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two rounds in this contest: Fall (October) and Spring (February–March) of the same academic year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both rounds occur in the same academic year; each round is a separate opportunity to compete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper levels, question counts and durations
rubrics_metrics.description: Both have an O-Level (Basic) paper and an A-Level (Advanced) paper separated by 1–2 weeks. The O-Level contains around 5 questions and the A-Level contains around 7 questions. The duration of the exams is 5 hours for both Levels. The A-Level problems are more difficult than O-Level but have a greater maximum score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: O-Level is basic; A-Level is advanced (harder, higher maximum). Exams are long (5 hours), so time management and depth of solutions matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant divisions and grade-based loadings
rubrics_metrics.description: Participating students are divided into two divisions; Junior (usually grades 7–10) and Senior (two last school grades, usually grades 11–12). To account for age differences inside of each division, students in different grades have different loadings (coefficients).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Division placement is by school grade; grading uses coefficients to adjust for age/grade differences within a division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per-paper scoring (choice of problems)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each paper the participant's score is the sum of his/her 3 best answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants may choose which problems to attempt; only their top three answers per paper count, encouraging strategic selection of problems and rewarding ingenuity over attempting all problems poorly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contestant final score across rounds
rubrics_metrics.description: A contestant's final score is his/her highest score from the four exams. It is not necessary albeit recommended to write all four exams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are up to four examinations (two rounds × two levels); the best single exam score is taken as the contestant's final score. Writing all exams is recommended but not mandatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Town handicaps and team scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Towns are given handicaps to account for differences in population. A town's score is the average of the scores of its N best students, where its population is N hundred thousand. It is also worth noting that the minimum value of N is 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Team/town comparisons use a population-based rule: N = population (in 100,000s), average the top N student scores, with N at least 5. This compensates for population disparities between towns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy and problem style
rubrics_metrics.description: Tournament of Towns differs from many other similar competitions by its philosophy relying much more upon ingenuity than the drill. First, problems are difficult (especially in A Level in the Senior division where they are comparable with those at International Mathematical Olympiad but much more ingenious and less technical). Second, it allows the participants to choose problems they like as for each paper the participant's score is the sum of his/her 3 best answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems are mostly combinatorial with occasional geometry, number theory or algebra; they favor ingenious, non-technical solutions. Expect a different flavor from other competitions and plan to focus on deep insight rather than routine techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards and diploma process
rubrics_metrics.description: Diplomas are awarded by the Central Committee to students who have achieved high scores (after their papers have been rechecked by the Central Jury). Different certificates are also awarded by Local Committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High scoring papers undergo rechecking by the Central Jury before Central Committee diplomas are issued; local committees may provide other certificates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summer Conference invitations for outstanding performers
rubrics_metrics.description: Students performing outstandingly (higher than Diploma) receive an invitation to the Annual International Mathematical Tournament of Towns Summer Conference where during several days they participate in team research projects consisting of the sequence of related problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top performers are invited to multi-day team research projects at the Annual Summer Conference—an opportunity for collaborative problem work beyond the contest itself.
